paragraphs.text: Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia type III (FHH3) is an autosomal dominant disorder of extracellular calcium homeostasis involving the parathyroids, kidneys, and bone. Like FHH1 and FHH2, it is characterized by lifelong elevation of serum calcium with inappropriately low urinary calcium excretion. Unlike FHH1 and FHH2, which usually have normal PTH, FHH3 features increased serum PTH, hypophosphatemia, and osteomalacia (Nesbit et al., 2013). Howles et al. (2016) described FHH3 as the most clinically severe of the 3 FHH types. It is caused by heterozygous AP2S1 mutations affecting arg15, and the mutant AP2-sigma proteins impair calcium-sensing receptor-mediated signal transduction.

paragraphs.text: McMurtry et al. (1992) described a large kindred with familial benign hypercalcemia (FBH). They surveyed 46 members across 5 generations, aged 1.5 to 91 years, by biochemical testing and/or chart review, and found 19 affected. In the 15 hypercalcemic subjects tested biochemically, serum immunoreactive PTH rose with age, became supranormal by about age 30 years, and appeared to increase further after that. Radiographic changes suggestive of osteomalacia were present in 3 of 5 affected adults older than 40 years who were studied. Two hypercalcemic adults had tetracycline-labeled iliac crest biopsies. In one of them, a 51-year-old woman, the biopsy confirmed defective skeletal mineralization. The authors suggested that the disorder may not be entirely benign and that osteomalacia, perhaps due to mild hypophosphatemia, can develop in adulthood.

The third was a 52-year-old woman with about 20 years of hypercalcemia who had headaches, abdominal pain, vomiting, fatigue, and musculoskeletal pain that did not resolve after pamidronate infusion or parathyroidectomy.

paragraphs.text: Hannan et al. (2010) performed linkage analysis in 34 informative members of the Oklahoma kindred, 19 of them affected, using 24 polymorphic loci (17 microsatellites and 7 SNPs). They found linkage to chromosome 19q13, with a peak 2-point LOD score of 6.92 at theta = 0 at D19S606. Recombinants in individuals II.2, III.3, and III.4 refined the FBHH3 locus to a 4.1-Mb interval (less than 10 cM) flanked by D19S112 and rs245111. This interval contains 135 protein-coding genes and 24 predicted genes. The syntenic region on mouse chromosome 7 contains 4 Casr-related sequences (Gprc2a-rs1, -rs2, -rs3, and -rs5), but Hannan et al. (2010) found no human or primate homologs of these sequences in the 19q13 region. Comparative analysis showed that 2 conserved segments are inverted in human, and that an 11.6-Mb mouse region containing 35 genes, including the 4 Gprc2a-rs genes, is absent from the human genome. The authors concluded that FBHH3 cannot be attributed to abnormalities of the Gprc2a-rs genes.

paragraphs.text: Nesbit et al. (2013) performed exome sequencing on 1 affected person from each of 2 unrelated FHH3 kindreds, from Oklahoma and from Northern Ireland. Dideoxynucleotide sequencing confirmed the variant, and restriction enzyme analysis showed that it cosegregated with the disorder in 32 affected and 23 unaffected members spanning 4 generations of the 2 kindreds. The authors then sequenced all 5 exons of AP2S1 in 50 unrelated FHH patients (23 males and 27 females) in whom CASR mutations had been excluded. They found 11 heterozygous missense mutations, all affecting arg15: 4 R15C, 3 R15H, and 4 R15L. Together with the 2 original kindreds, this gave 13 unrelated probands with arg15 mutations. Arg15 was significantly conserved in 5,400 human exomes (p less than 10(-10)), which the authors took to indicate a likely mutational hotspot. Functional studies showed that the mutants reduced the sensitivity of CaSR-expressing cells to extracellular calcium and reduced CaSR endocytosis (see PATHOGENESIS).

paragraphs.text: Nesbit et al. (2013) expressed the R15C, R15H, and R15L AP2S1 mutants in HEK293 cells stably expressing CaSR. All 3 raised the EC50 for extracellular calcium (2.90, 2.73, and 2.86 mM vs 2.53 mM for wildtype; p less than 0.0001), indicating reduced sensitivity to extracellular calcium, as seen with FHH1 CASR mutations. The cys15 mutant gave an EC50 significantly higher than vector alone, which the authors suggested indicates a possible dominant-negative effect. Intact-cell ELISA showed that, after stimulation with extracellular calcium, cells transfected with wildtype AP2S1 lost more surface CaSR than cells transfected with the R15C mutant or vector alone. They noted that AP2-sigma-2 is ubiquitously expressed, yet its arg15 mutations cause a specific disorder of calcium homeostasis rather than a multisystem disease. They suggested that arg15 has a specific role, such as recognizing the CaSR dileucine motif, and that mutations at other AP2S1 residues might cause different diseases.

paragraphs.text: Nesbit et al. (2013) performed exome sequencing on affected members of 2 unrelated FHH3 kindreds, from Oklahoma and from Northern Ireland. In both, they identified a heterozygous C-to-T transition in exon 2 of the AP2S1 gene that results in an arg15-to-cys (R15C) substitution. Restriction enzyme analysis showed that the mutation cosegregated with the disorder in 32 affected and 23 unaffected members spanning 4 generations of the 2 kindreds. They also found R15C in 4 of 50 unrelated FHH patients without CASR mutations. In HEK293 cells stably expressing CaSR, the R15C mutant raised the EC50 for extracellular calcium (2.90 mM vs 2.53 mM for wildtype), and the EC50 was significantly higher than with vector alone, suggesting a possible dominant-negative effect. After stimulation with extracellular calcium, cells transfected with the R15C mutant lost less surface CaSR than cells transfected with wildtype AP2S1, indicating reduced CaSR endocytosis.
